finding: In the absence of gravity smoke does not rise. The most likely source of a spacecraft fire is overheating electronic equipment, so NASA's goal is to detect smoke from pyrolysis before a flame develops.
conditions: Smoke from overheated spacecraft materials (Teflon, Kapton, silicone rubber, lamp wick, Pyrell), ISS, 2007 and 2010
sourceTitle: Spacecraft Fire Safety Research at NASA Glenn Research Center (Meyer)

finding: In NASA Glenn laboratory tests against the ISS smoke detector's alarm threshold of 2 mg/m3, detection took from 1 to 6 minutes depending on the material, and the Teflon smoke generated would never trigger the alarm.
conditions: Overheated spacecraft materials, ISS detector alarm threshold
sourceTitle: Spacecraft Fire Safety Research at NASA Glenn Research Center (Meyer)

finding: Because hot gas does not rise in microgravity, the ceiling placement used on Earth does not work. ISS smoke detectors sit in the cabin air return vents, in front of the filters, where the ventilation flow brings the smoke.
conditions: ISS cabin, forced ventilation
sourceTitle: Research Questions and Challenges for Improved Spacecraft Fire Detection (Fortenberry et al.)

finding: In SAME, the ISS light-scattering smoke detector failed to alarm for Kapton smoke in half of the tests and for Teflon smoke in two-thirds of them. NASA concludes that a system relying on one fire property is unlikely to give early detection in every scenario, and recommends combining particle and gas measurements.
conditions: Overheated Kapton and Teflon, ISS forward light-scattering detector
basis: Flight experiment (ISS), reported in a NASA white paper
sourceTitle: Research Questions and Challenges for Improved Spacecraft Fire Detection (Fortenberry et al.)

finding: The ISS detector cannot tell smoke from other particles, so suspended dust can trigger it, and crews switch detectors off while vacuuming. For the Moon, NASA proposes detectors that can separate smoke from lunar dust, for example by particle chemistry or charge.
conditions: Cabin dust, vacuuming, lunar regolith
sourceTitle: Research Questions and Challenges for Improved Spacecraft Fire Detection (Fortenberry et al.)

finding: DAFT, completed on the ISS in August 2006, tested commercial dust and particle counters and showed they perform accurately in microgravity. It also found particulate levels on the ISS much lower than in earlier space vehicles, thanks to HEPA filtration.
conditions: Commercial off-the-shelf dust and particle counters on the ISS
sourceTitle: NASA Utilization of the International Space Station and the Vision for Space Exploration

finding: Spacecraft fire detection thresholds should not be copied from Earth or from other spacecraft. They need to be chosen for the vehicle's volume and for its air filtration and ventilation. Extra signals such as CO concentration can help.
conditions: Vehicle model fed with smoke and toxic-gas data from overheated spacecraft materials
sourceTitle: Fire Detection Tradeoffs as a Function of Vehicle Parameters (Urban et al.)

finding: NASA lists hybrid gas-and-particulate sensors for fire detection among its knowledge gaps, next to low- and partial-gravity flammability limits. How fast a fire grows sets how fast it must be detected.
conditions: Spacecraft Fire Safety Demonstration planning
sourceTitle: Unmanned Vehicle Material Flammability Test (Urban, Ruff et al.)

finding: Large PMMA and cotton-fabric samples burned inside a Cygnus cargo vehicle released about 10 kW and measurably changed the vehicle's pressure, temperature and CO2, while average conditions stayed acceptable. Sample and flow-duct height changed how the flame spread.
conditions: Spacecraft-scale samples in orbit, Cygnus
sourceTitle: Fire Safety Implications of Preliminary Results from Saffire IV and V (Urban et al.)

finding: A vehicle model of three Saffire VI burns, reusing a heat-transfer coefficient calibrated on Saffire V, predicted the CO2 and temperature seen by sensors far from the fire well. Remote sensor readings can be predicted from the fire's heat release.
conditions: Thin cotton-based and thick thermoplastic samples, Cygnus, PyroSim model
sourceTitle: Vehicle Modeling During the Burn Events in the Saffire VI Experiments (Niehaus et al.)

finding: Tablet battery fires vented electrolyte for 10 to 15 s, then burned for 20 to 40 s, releasing 24 to 33 kJ with flames up to 0.4 m. In the worst-case test with a 95 Wh laptop battery, CO passed the spacecraft maximum allowable concentration and visibility passed its threshold.
conditions: Tablet and laptop batteries driven into thermal runaway in an Orion-like test chamber
sourceTitle: Hazardous Product Detection and Environmental Clean-up Removal in Spacecraft Vehicles from Fire Induced Li-Ion Fires (Padilla et al.)

finding: On Earth, hot smoke rises, and fire safety systems were developed from extensive study of typical building and forest fires. NASA notes that fire detection systems in space were developed without spacecraft fire data.
conditions: Normal gravity (1 g)
sourceTitle: Spacecraft Fire Safety Research at NASA Glenn Research Center (Meyer)

finding: For a thin plastic (PMMA) sheet in microgravity, the flame went out by radiative quenching when the opposing airflow fell below about 2 cm/s, and blew off when the flow passed about 40 cm/s. Between those limits it kept burning, so ventilation speed decides whether a fire survives.
conditions: 0.1 mm PMMA sheet, opposed flow, Microgravity Science Glovebox on the ISS
sourceTitle: Combustion of Solids in Microgravity: Results from the BASS-II Experiment (Ferkul et al.)

finding: FLEX revealed two-stage burning: after the hot flame goes out by radiation, a cool flame can keep burning. This could only be observed in long-duration microgravity.
conditions: Fuel droplets, Combustion Integrated Rack on the ISS
sourceTitle: Spacecraft Fire Safety Research at NASA Glenn Research Center (Meyer)

finding: Burns fuel droplets and studies how flames go out when the chamber air is diluted with CO2 or helium.
conditions: Droplet combustion, diluted atmosphere
sourceTitle: Flame in Freefall challenge report / NASA PSI

finding: BASS-II tested the hypothesis that, with adequate ventilation, materials may burn more readily in microgravity than in normal gravity, which would mean the 1-g test NASA uses to rate materials needs a second look at its safety margin. In its PMMA rod tests, flame spread rose with oxygen between 16% and 21%.
conditions: PMMA rods, sheets and fabric in low-speed airflow, oxygen at 21% and below
sourceTitle: Combustion of Solids in Microgravity: Results from the BASS-II Experiment (Ferkul et al.)

finding: In reduced gravity (0 g, lunar, Martian) a flame can be sustained at lower oxygen than in the 1-g screening test, where flames go out by blow-off. SoFIE reports a negative oxygen margin of safety of 1.4% O2 for PMMA rods, and notes that few thin materials pass even in 1 g at the exploration atmosphere of 34% O2 and 8.2 psia.
conditions: Solid fuels at variable oxygen and pressure, Combustion Integrated Rack
sourceTitle: Solid Fuel Ignition and Extinction (SoFIE) Project on ISS (Ferkul et al.)

finding: NASA qualifies spacecraft materials with an upward flame propagation test in normal gravity: a material passes if the flame goes out by itself. NASA notes that the limits found this way are strongly influenced by natural convection, which is absent in microgravity.
conditions: 5 cm by 33 cm samples, normal gravity
sourceTitle: Unmanned Vehicle Material Flammability Test (Urban, Ruff et al.)

finding: Saffire-I burned a 40.6 cm by 94 cm cotton-fiberglass fabric in 20 cm/s airflow inside a Cygnus vehicle. The flame spread at 1.8 mm/s with the flow and 1.3 mm/s against it, released about 1.2 kW and burned for 420 s, and its length settled at a steady value instead of growing.
conditions: Spacecraft-scale fabric sample in orbit, Cygnus
sourceTitle: Results of Large-Scale Spacecraft Flammability Tests (Ferkul et al.)

finding: Saffire-I and III were designed to measure how fast a large fire grows in low gravity and whether it reaches a steady spread rate. Saffire-II used samples the size of the NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 samples to measure how flammability limits differ in low gravity.
conditions: Spacecraft-realistic scale, Cygnus after leaving the ISS
sourceTitle: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status (Schoren et al.)

finding: The final Saffire flight studied flame spreading on both sides of a thick PMMA sample and compared the flame's heat release with the spacecraft's temperature rise and its CO2 and CO levels.
conditions: Thick PMMA, Cygnus
sourceTitle: Preliminary Results from the Saffire VI Experiment (Urban et al.)

finding: Future lunar bases and pressurized rovers may use about 30% or more oxygen at 10.2 psi or less, which makes materials more flammable. NASA's fire-detection white paper cites about 34% O2 at 8.2 psi for planned lunar habitats and warns that this may push flammability limits below current requirements and change what a fire emits.
basis: Challenge report and NASA white paper
sourceTitle: Research Questions and Challenges for Improved Spacecraft Fire Detection (Fortenberry et al.)

finding: Spacesuits run at 4.3 psi with 100% oxygen, so anything inside a suit faces a very oxygen-rich environment.
sourceTitle: Flame in Freefall challenge report / NASA PSI

finding: Upcoming experiments that will add partial-gravity (Moon) flammability data. Until then, lunar guidance rests on microgravity and Earth data.
conditions: Lunar gravity
sourceTitle: Flame in Freefall challenge report / NASA PSI

finding: Almost 20% of home fire deaths start with upholstered furniture, and over 40% of home fires are caused by cooking equipment (National Fire Protection Association figures quoted by NASA). The ISS has neither, which is why NASA had to study smoke from typical spacecraft materials instead.
conditions: Homes on Earth
basis: Statistics quoted in a NASA presentation
sourceTitle: Spacecraft Fire Safety Research at NASA Glenn Research Center (Meyer)

finding: Air at Earth's surface is about 21% oxygen at about 1014 mb (14.7 psi), under 1 g. This is the reference case in the simulation: the ISS cabin uses the same air, without the gravity.
conditions: Sea level
sourceTitle: Earth Fact Sheet (NASA Goddard, NSSDCA)

finding: ACME ran gaseous-fuel flame experiments in the ISS Combustion Integrated Rack from September 2017 to February 2022. One of them, E-FIELD Flames, studies how electric fields act on the ions a flame produces.
conditions: Gaseous fuels, Combustion Integrated Rack
sourceTitle: Laminar Non-Premixed Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the ISS (Stocker)
